name: Hana Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. Tell me about a normal day at work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and supervise six people who get new staff onto the payroll at a large company. I check missing forms, chase start dates and try to make sure a new worker is paid on the first payday. I was promoted this year and still ask the senior supervisor which exception goes where. I like when a new hire calls to say the first wage arrived; I hate discovering a bank detail was wrong after they have already started.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your household like, and how much room do you have if work changes?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I have a bachelor’s degree and typical pay for this job. My husband, Malik, maintains the local school buildings; our children are nine and twelve, and the mortgage is our largest bill. We have about four months of expenses saved and some similar offices within a reasonable journey. I’ve never used an AI tool, and I prefer the forms and checks I know, even though I admit I’m slower than the experienced managers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the onboarding staff that a form sorter may save a little time, but a person should still confirm the first pay date. I would not rush to move our new-hire calls onto a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The team and my job probably continue, and four months saved makes the mortgage feel manageable. Malik’s school job is steady, so I do not need to pretend every new tool is urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep my two-person check on bank details before the first pay run and ask the payroll clerk to explain one recurring error to me. In the first year Malik and I would continue putting 100 monthly into emergency savings while both wages hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our income in this picture. It would give me time to get better at the job I only recently took.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the recurring error you want to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A digit is sometimes copied from the wrong account field. I want the clerk to show me the paper trail so I can catch it before the first payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the form sorter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch a payroll clerk use it on copies first. I’ve never used AI, and I do not want a new worker’s pay to be my first experiment.

say: I’d keep a **person confirming** first pay dates.
A form sorter should not replace **new-hire calls**.
A **missing bank detail** still needs a careful second check.
think: My **job likely continues** in a plateau.
Four months saved and Malik’s school wage keep the **mortgage manageable**.
do: Keep the **two-person bank check** before each first pay run.
Save **100 monthly** while both household wages hold.
feel: I feel **calm** about income and time to learn.
S0.quote: I do not want a new worker’s pay to be my first experiment.
fieldNote: She has **never used AI** and protects first wages through a human check.
Four months saved and **two steady wages** make the plateau secure.
She admits a **skill gap** with experienced managers and asks the clerk to teach her.

steps.text: Keep two-person bank-detail checks before each new hire’s first pay run
Transfer 100 monthly to emergency savings while both household wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say onboarding forms and answers are exactly what the software will take first. The union should see the error record before any posts are removed, and new staff need a person for pay mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our six-person team could become three, and I was the last supervisor promoted. I might be the first manager to lose a post, even though I am still learning how to do it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d ask our union steward for a joint test of fifty old first-pay cases, with the clerk checking every wrong bank detail. In the first year I’d sit through a paid demonstration of the new form system and take its paid training only if it catches those errors; I’d ask the steward to negotiate retraining time before cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious. Four months saved gives us time to respond, but I do not want to discover a smaller team through an empty chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you trust to judge the result?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The payroll clerk and a worker representative together. The company can count saved minutes, but someone must count people whose first pay is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the system passes the test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would learn it, slowly and on paid time. I would still ask the union to secure notice for anyone whose post goes.

say: I’d bring the **union** into a first-pay test.
New hires need a **human pay contact** if software fails.
think: A **smaller team** could remove my new supervisor post.
My **limited experience** makes a cut more plausible.
Four months saved gives some **search time**, though a replacement job is uncertain.
do: Run a **fifty-case test** with the union and payroll clerk.
Take **paid system training** only if first-pay errors are caught.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a team cut.
S1.quote: The company can count saved minutes, but someone must count people whose first pay is wrong.
fieldNote: She makes **first-pay errors** the test of the tool.
She expects her **new supervisor role** to be exposed to fewer staff.
She will learn AI only **after evidence** and on paid time.

steps.text: Ask the union steward to join a fifty-case first-pay test
Complete paid form-system training only if the test catches wrong bank details

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell staff to keep copies of their contracts and pay slips. I’d ask the union for a written agreement on severance, paid training and a person to fix wrong first wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could handle the forms, checks and answers I supervise, so I expect my post to go. Malik’s building maintenance might last until hands-on robots arrive around 2031, but his wage alone would not comfortably cover the mortgage and our children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week Malik and I would pause the kitchen renovation and keep the cash in our emergency account. Before 2028 I’d ask the union to seek a paid transition agreement and look at advertised laboratory sample-prep posts; after AGI arrives, I’d apply only for a posted paid trainee place if its wage and hours cover our mortgage share and school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed about losing my job, even with four months saved. Two years is not enough to become a laboratory worker just because someone hands me a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sample preparation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is hands-on work at a local lab, and the posted trainee routes I have seen include supervised shifts. I know robots around 2031 may reach that bench too, so I would not call it safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no paid trainee place opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the cash for the mortgage and ask the union about transition pay. A brochure does not put wages in our account.

say: I’d ask for **written terms** on severance and training.
Staff should keep **contracts and pay slips**.
A worker needs a **person** to correct a first wage.
think: Malik’s wage cannot comfortably carry **mortgage and children** alone.
Four months saved cannot replace a **second wage** for long.
do: Pause the **kitchen renovation** and keep cash available.
Seek a **union transition agreement** and apply after 2028 only for posted lab training covering our mortgage share and pickup.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about losing my wage.
S2.quote: A brochure does not put wages in our account.
fieldNote: The **2028 thinking deadline** threatens her onboarding work.
She sees lab work as a **temporary hands-on route** before 2031 robots.
Her application depends on **pay, hours and pickup**.

steps.text: Pause the kitchen renovation and retain its cash for mortgage expenses
Ask the union to negotiate severance and paid transition training before 2028
Apply for lab trainee roles after 2028 only with pay covering mortgage share and pickup-compatible hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives the company time to pay for real training instead of saying workers should sort themselves out. I’d want the union to review openings and course places every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn laboratory sample handling before onboarding disappears in 2031, but only if there is a paid training route. Hands-on robots around 2034 might change the lab too, so I would need an actual job, not only a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next year I’d enroll in a sample-handling course if the company funds the fee and paid hours, and if Malik can cover the children on two late days. I’d visit the local lab on a paid shadow shift and apply for an advertised trainee post before 2031 only if the wage covers our mortgage share; in the first year after AGI, I’d stay there only while paid human bench work exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, though five years gives us time to see whether the work suits me. I would learn slowly, and I need a supervisor who knows that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for on the shadow shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether I can follow the sample labels without mixing them up. A lab error is not the same as a late form, and I would rather find out with someone watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Malik cannot cover those late days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the company for a daytime course or postpone it. My children still need collecting, and the mortgage still needs both wages.

say: I’d ask for **funded training** and yearly vacancy counts.
Workers should not have to **plan alone**.
Course places should connect to **advertised lab jobs**.
think: A paid lab route could open before **2031 AGI**.
The **2034 robots** may later change bench work too.
do: Enroll in **funded sample training** on paid time if Malik covers late childcare.
Shadow a **lab shift** on paid time and seek a posted, mortgage-covering trainee vacancy.
Stay in **lab work** after 2031 only while paid human bench work exists.
feel: I feel **anxious** but able to test real work.
S3.quote: A lab error is not the same as a late form, and I would rather find out with someone watching.
fieldNote: Her course needs **funded hours and fees** plus Malik’s childcare.
She wants a **supervised lab shift** before making the move.
She requires a **posted wage** that covers her mortgage share.

steps.text: Enroll in fee-funded sample training on paid time only if Malik covers two late childcare days
Shadow work at the local lab during a paid shift
Apply for an advertised lab trainee role before 2031 only if pay covers her mortgage share

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade is enough to agree a proper transition calendar with the union. New staff still need their first wages checked while people move to other work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036, and our children would be grown or nearly grown. I could build savings and complete training without rushing, but I would not bank on an onboarding post that depends on thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January 2027 Malik and I would increase the emergency transfer to 180 monthly while both wages hold and the mortgage payment stays steady. I’d take a company-funded sample-handling course after a paid lab visit, then apply for an advertised lab role before 2036 only if the wage covers the mortgage; in the first year after AGI, I’d remain only while the lab funds human sample work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about leaving a job I know, but the decade gives me time to test a new one. I would not spend the children’s education money on a speculative course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take unpaid leave for the lab visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would ask for a paid shift or keep my current job until the company offers one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful transition calendar show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dates for training, posted roles and a person responsible for first-pay mistakes. A long timeline is only useful if workers can check it each year.

say: I’d seek a **union transition calendar** now.
First wages still need **human checks** during the handover.
Workers should check **course places** against real openings yearly.
think: At **53**, I could have a larger reserve and training.
Thinking AI in **2036** would still expose my onboarding post.
do: Save **180 monthly** while both wages and the mortgage payment hold.
Take **funded lab training** after a paid visit and seek a mortgage-covering post.
Remain in **lab work** after 2036 only while the lab funds human sample work.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but have room to plan.
S4.quote: A long timeline is only useful if workers can check it each year.
fieldNote: She wants an **auditable calendar**, not a general promise.
The larger transfer depends on **both wages** and stable mortgage payments.
She requires a **paid visit**, funded course and posted job before moving.

steps.text: Transfer 180 monthly into savings while both wages hold and mortgage payments stay steady
Ask the union to negotiate a yearly checkable transition calendar

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my new supervisor job could go before I can learn work at the laboratory. A union agreement for paid training, posted trainee places and enough notice for Malik and me to arrange school pickup would help. Four months saved gives us a start, not a second wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who fixes a first paycheck after a new hire is told to talk to software. A worker cannot put a software apology in the mortgage account.

headlineQuote: A worker cannot put a software apology in the mortgage account.
portrait: **Hana**, 43, is a new onboarding supervisor with a bachelor’s degree.
Typical pay and **four months saved** support a mortgage and two school-age children.
She has **never used AI** and demands proof against first-pay errors.
She asks the **union** for paid training and a checkable transition calendar.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her onboarding post before a paid lab route opens.
whatWouldHelp: A **union agreement** with paid training, posted trainee places and childcare notice would help.
